title: The Distant Silence
premise: Hazel Nakamura, a translator who has spent thirty years burying the language of her childhood—and the memory of what happened the summer her family's village was displaced—receives a letter from Marisol Aun, the last fluent speaker of that tongue, asking Hazel to become her final student. Returning to the fading coastal town, Hazel finds Marisol's memory failing faster than her lessons can hold it, and discovers the old woman was a witness to the betrayal Hazel has spent her life not remembering: her own father's testimony helped condemn the village. As Marisol dies, Hazel must choose whether to carry the language forward as inheritance or indictment, and she ends by teaching it—imperfectly, aloud—to her estranged daughter, accepting that survival is a debt paid in voice.
about_author: Kestrel Yarrow is the pen name of a former court interpreter who spent a decade documenting endangered languages across the Pacific Rim before turning to fiction. They live quietly on an island where three languages are spoken and two are dying.

chapters.title: The Smile That Ends Conversations
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. In Vancouver, Hazel works as a translator of safe, living languages, deflecting every question about her own childhood tongue with practiced charm. A letter arrives in handwriting she almost recognizes. The emotional beat is the first crack in her armor—the reader sees how much effort invisibility costs her.

chapters.title: A Letter in a Dying Alphabet
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV, with flashbacks. She deciphers Marisol Aun's letter, written partly in the language Hazel pretends not to know, asking for one final student before 'the words go back to sleep.' Hazel burns the letter, then retrieves it from the sink. The beat is denial curdling into compulsion.

chapters.title: The Road Back Is Underwater
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. She travels to the coastal town of Port Anselm, half-claimed by rising water, where the old village site is now a gated resort. Marisol, sharp-tongued and ninety-one, refuses to teach until Hazel admits why she left. The beat is friction between two women guarding the same wound.

chapters.title: First Words, Old Wounds
chapters.summary: Alternating POV begins: Marisol's chapters surface memories Hazel never heard. Lessons start badly—Hazel's fluency returns too fast, revealing she lied about forgetting. Marisol names her a coward but keeps teaching. The beat is shame transformed into hunger.

chapters.title: What the Father Signed
chapters.summary: Marisol's POV dominates. She reveals that Hazel's father, as a young interpreter, provided the testimony used to strip the village of its land—a betrayal he may have been coerced into. Hazel finds his signature in the county archive. The beat is the collapse of the innocent-dead-parent myth.

chapters.title: The Resort and the Ruin
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. The resort developer, courting Marisol for a 'heritage branding' deal, offers money to record the language as corporate property. Hazel, needing funds for Marisol's care, is tempted. The beat is power's soft corruption—survival offered at the price of ownership.

chapters.title: Marisol Forgets the Word for River
chapters.summary: Dual POV. Dementia accelerates; Marisol begins losing the language mid-sentence, and Hazel records desperately, sometimes feeding her words like blood. Their intimacy deepens into something like motherhood. The beat is grief running ahead of death.

chapters.title: The Testimony
chapters.summary: Climax approaches. Hazel uncovers the full recording of her father's testimony and hears him weep as he translates lies—he was translating under threat, protecting Hazel's mother by obeying. Marisol, lucid one last evening, asks Hazel to read it aloud in the original language. The beat is devastating, complicated forgiveness.

chapters.title: The Last Speaker
chapters.summary: Climax. Marisol dies during a storm, mid-lesson, leaving Hazel holding a language with no second speaker and the developer's contract unsigned on the table. Hazel tears it up and instead donates the recordings to the community descendants, surrendering control. The beat is loss transfigured into release.

chapters.title: Teaching My Daughter the Word for Home
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV, epilogue a year later. In her kitchen, Hazel teaches her wary, adult daughter the first ten words, laughing at her own mistakes, the smile that ended conversations finally retired. The language survives imperfectly, carried by flawed hands. The beat is quiet hope: memory kept alive by being shared, not guarded.
